title: Persistent allograft dysfunction: cause-defining investigation
fairness: Kidney-allograft core biopsy is the best listed investigation after persistent dysfunction despite volume correction and the represented structural assessment. Plasma BK testing remains useful concurrently; the item does not need to imply that it should be omitted.

The resident must interpret the residual unexplained dysfunction, then choose tissue classification rather than equate missed doses with rejection. The alternatives are parallel investigations. Necessary flow, drainage and exposure findings do not yield a reliable nonmedical phrase match.
The current single-node case stands alone; its presentation supplies age and sex and its task specifies persistent graft dysfunction. No later executable treatment node remains in this case.

Review scope: all 19 current executable candidates (17 new and 2 rewrites), including the 8 preserved candidate versions, were independently assessed from presentation, update, task, options and explanation. No separate exhibit is present. The original 3 kept records, 29 proposed retired/replacement input records, held/unkeyed material and 4 parked corrections are noted but excluded from verdicts. Review-only keys and author gate claims were not evidence of quality.

This is an offline editorial review, not source verification or clinical approval. PASS does not change needs_clinician_review or replace Melissa Rowland's exact-version sign-off. Difficulty and highYield are qualitative judgments, not measured performance or verified examination-frequency claims. Runtime rendering, randomization and wait metadata are outside this visible-text review.
suggestions: Preserve the distinction between prioritizing biopsy and also obtaining indicated viral tests.

title: Escalation after persistent cellular graft injury
fairness: Rabbit antithymocyte globulin is the best listed escalation for continued deterioration after completed steroids with repeat cellular injury and the represented negative viral/humoral reassessment. The phrasing 'consider' avoids an unconditional rescue prescription.

Two consequential steps remain: reclassify persistent injury using repeat tissue rather than steroid nonresponse alone, then select cellular rescue instead of humoral treatment or maintenance reduction. This is high-yield rejection management.

The summary 'does not support an antibody-mediated component' makes elimination easier, but still requires knowledge of the competing treatments; it does not create a nonmedical unique-word match. The specific treatment choices are comparable.
The standalone update includes prior steroid treatment and repeat findings; the opening 'A later record' does not require another scored question to establish the timeline.

title: Isolated BK viruria and maintenance treatment
fairness: Maintaining the regimen with repeat plasma testing is the best listed plan for urinary detection with negative contemporaneous plasma testing and stable function. No unsupported numerical treatment threshold or interval is asserted.

Interpreting specimen compartments and then deciding whether to accept rejection risk from maintenance reduction are consequential steps. Immediate reduction is a credible error; leflunomide is a weaker treatment misconception.
All choices share 'repeat plasma BK testing', so that phrase does not disclose the key. The result and stable function require clinical interpretation rather than grammatical elimination.
First part is self-contained. Its explanation teaches the significance of the present urinary finding without naming the later biopsy-proven treatment.

title: Biopsy-supported BK nephropathy: treatment direction
fairness: Stepwise maintenance reduction is the best listed direction given persistent plasma detection, tissue inclusions/staining, low immunologic risk and the represented absence of concurrent rejection. Steroid escalation and cidofovir are not equally supported routine alternatives in this setting.

The resident interprets tissue plus blood findings and applies the infection-versus-rejection balance to treatment. This remains moderate, not hard: the integrated exclusion of rejection reduces competing uncertainty.
No reliable wording, length, absolute or convergence shortcut selects the key. Low immunologic risk is a necessary treatment boundary, although it is supplied as a clinical summary.

The later admission follows the first BK node coherently and includes all findings necessary for independent selection. Earlier feedback scaffolds compartment interpretation but does not give this treatment answer.
suggestions: Keep the low-risk and no-concurrent-rejection boundaries attached to this version; do not generalize its treatment to every BK-positive recipient.

title: Progressing lymphadenopathy despite falling EBV DNA
fairness: Representative lymph-node tissue is the best listed cause-defining investigation for enlarging/multisite nodes after a nondiagnostic aspirate. A falling blood EBV result cannot classify the lesion; PET/CT may later assist staging but does not replace tissue diagnosis.

The consequential reasoning is to reconcile discordant blood and lesion trajectories, then choose a diagnostic specimen rather than repeat surveillance or move directly to staging. This is a high-yield PTLD and lymphoma diagnostic principle.

The aspirate's inability to classify the process is necessary adequacy evidence rather than an invented missing-test cue. The choices are investigations of comparable specificity without a key-only explanatory qualifier.
The current standalone case supplies the earlier sampling result, subsequent progression and transplant context. It does not depend on removed companion nodes.

title: Persistent gastrointestinal symptoms with negative plasma CMV testing
fairness: Ileocolonoscopy with mucosal biopsy best distinguishes the represented mucosal differential, including tissue-invasive CMV and medication injury. Repeated negative blood testing does not settle tissue disease. A cellular-immunity assay does not provide a competing tissue diagnosis.

The resident must reject false reassurance from blood testing and choose a test that distinguishes remaining mucosal causes. This is a useful transplant infection decision; the two other blood-focused choices make it moderate rather than hard.

No direct lexical cue names the biopsy. The repeated plasma assay is a weaker distractor because it has already been performed, but it still represents a recognizable mistaken reliance on blood surveillance. Do not count its repetition as an independent hard discriminator.

The standalone update includes persistent symptoms, prior tests, medication and structural context. 'Antiviral treatment records' in the presentation anticipates the broader record but neither establishes the cause of this episode nor supplies the investigation.
suggestions: For a future harder variant, compare tissue evaluation with a genuinely plausible competing diagnostic or medication strategy; do not add more negative tests just to lengthen the stem.

title: Cytopenias after adding allopurinol to azathioprine
fairness: Stopping allopurinol is the best listed additional medication change while the service addresses cytopenias and the azathioprine regimen. Substitution with febuxostat preserves the important xanthine-oxidase interaction concern; reducing tacrolimus does not address the represented temporal pattern.

The resident identifies the interaction from chronology and then avoids a same-class substitution error. The febuxostat alternative gives this high-yield drug interaction more than simple culprit recognition.

The task's 'additional' wording is justified by the shared active assessment of azathioprine; it does not mean stopping allopurinol is the complete cytopenia management plan. No option is a uniquely cautious composite answer.

The standalone update explicitly supplies the regimen, added medicine and blood-count changes; 'A later record' is understandable without the former pregnancy companion. The explanation appropriately acknowledges management-strategy differences without inventing a dose.

title: Tacrolimus during recovering delayed graft function
fairness: Continuing the represented tacrolimus regimen is the best listed plan given improving output/creatinine, tissue-supported tubular injury and verified target-range exposure. Earlier dialysis alone does not establish ongoing CNI toxicity or justify a routine switch to sirolimus.

The resident interprets the recovery trajectory against the earlier dialysis requirement, then decides whether the existing regimen needs alteration. This is a practical high-yield distinction between delayed function and an indication to withdraw immunosuppression.

Continue/withhold/replace options are parallel specific plans. The target-range result is relevant but is not presented as universally excluding CNI injury. No reliable nonmedical cue selects the key.
The case is now standalone and includes the biopsy and trajectory it requires; 'subsequent biopsy' does not leave a decision-critical prior result missing.

title: Initial therapy for untreated cellular graft injury
fairness: Intravenous methylprednisolone is the best listed initial treatment for the represented untreated interstitial/tubular cellular process without the described arterial, viral or humoral component. The explicit arterial sampling repairs an important severity ambiguity without inventing a Banff grade.
The resident interprets the biopsy and competing infection/humoral findings, then distinguishes initial steroid therapy from lymphocyte-depleting rescue. These are consequential high-yield decisions.

The negatives are extensive and lower difficulty, but they establish relevant treatment boundaries; there is no key-only wording overlap or option-length advantage. The task prespecifies antirejection treatment appropriately for choosing among three such regimens.

The current update retains persistent dysfunction and the treatment-naive stage, so the standalone node no longer needs a preceding biopsy-selection question. No confident clinical inaccuracy is identified; exact pathology/severity ranking still needs clinician sign-off.
suggestions: Consider tightening the report wording without removing the represented arterial assessment, infection studies or initial-treatment boundary.

title: Renewed graft dysfunction after BK treatment
fairness: Repeat allograft biopsy is the best listed cause-defining plan before increasing or further decreasing maintenance therapy. Prior biopsy-proven BK and subsequent plasma clearance do not identify the cause of renewed dysfunction.

The resident must interpret the discordance between viral and renal trajectories, then avoid opposite empiric immunosuppression changes with different hazards. The prior initial improvement is useful chronology, not decorative detail.

The biopsy choice is the only investigation, but this does not automatically invalidate the option set: the case supplies a real unresolved discrepancy that determines whether an empiric drug change is justified. 'Graft-assessment plan' mildly favors evaluation; it is not a deterministic match because the other plans also include follow-up creatinine.

The standalone node includes the prior biopsy, treatment, response and new deterioration. The earlier BK case need not be seen. This is high-yield graft dysfunction reasoning with no asserted universal BK threshold.
suggestions: Use a neutral lead-in such as 'Which next plan best fits the renewed graft dysfunction?' to avoid even the mild investigation bias from 'graft-assessment plan'.

title: Renewed dysfunction after correction of a tacrolimus interaction
fairness: Allograft tissue is the best listed next step after the earlier exposure problem improves and renal dysfunction subsequently recurs despite valid target-range levels and the represented initial assessment. Neither further reduction nor restoration of the earlier dose follows from creatinine alone.

The resident must separate the earlier drug-interaction episode from the current unexplained course, then choose tissue assessment rather than another unsupported dose-direction change. This meets two-step reasoning and tests a high-yield anchoring error.

The different plan types are justified by a genuine unresolved causal discrepancy. The task does not name biopsy, and the explanation expressly avoids claiming that a target trough excludes all CNI injury or that dose reduction proves rejection.

The standalone chronology is coherent and complete. The interaction facts support the earlier episode rather than diagnose the renewed decline. This substantially overlaps the general renal-biopsy construct, which is a coverage consideration rather than a fairness failure.
suggestions: Keep the initial response followed by renewed deterioration; shortening this to a single high tacrolimus concentration would change the decision.

title: Tacrolimus dosing after a mistimed concentration
fairness: Continuing the monitored current dose while obtaining a valid predose level is the best listed plan given a postdose sample, unchanged renal function, no represented toxicity symptoms and no other medication change. The flagged value does not establish an excessive trough.

The resident interprets sampling validity and then uses the stable clinical course to choose continuation rather than precautionary dose reduction or withholding. The added treatment decision is consequential; it is not merely choosing the definition of a trough.

The shared repeat-level clause in all three choices prevents monitoring wording from identifying the answer. The explicitly stated postdose timing is necessary data, not an unfair disclosure of the dose decision.

The standalone update supplies timing, clinical trajectory and the imminent dosing decision. This is a common medication-monitoring pitfall. Its difficulty is toward the easier end of moderate; no numerical toxicity threshold is asserted.
suggestions: Preserve the stable-function and symptom context so the answer is not generalized to an ill patient merely because one specimen was mistimed.

title: CMV discharge therapy: route and treatment phase
fairness: Oral valganciclovir at renal-adjusted treatment dosing is the best listed discharge plan with improving gastrointestinal symptoms, demonstrated oral intake and persistent quantifiable CMV above the stated endpoint. Continued treatment does not itself require IV delivery.

Two consequential distinctions remain: infer adequate oral delivery from the clinical response, then distinguish unfinished treatment from prevention. The balanced four-cell matrix does not select the key by majority-component convergence.

'Scheduled oral medicines taken without vomiting' supports two oral options, while the unfinished virologic course supports two treatment-dose options. Neither phrase uniquely identifies the answer without integrating both observations. The intake observations are decision-critical, not gratuitous permission.

The standalone update contains the diagnosis, initial severe delivery problem, improvement and remaining treatment indication. The task is complete. No universal viral-load endpoint is invented; clinician review should retain the represented clinical improvement when accepting the route switch.

title: Medication adjustment during CMV-associated treatment neutropenia
fairness: Temporarily holding mycophenolate while retaining renal-adjusted valganciclovir is the best listed interim plan for the specified neutropenia during unfinished treatment, with low immunologic risk and count support/reassessment being arranged.

The resident interprets the neutrophil trajectory in a multiple-drug setting, then preserves antiviral treatment exposure while addressing another marrow suppressant. Lowering an otherwise appropriate treatment dose or treating active disease with letermovir are not equally supported alternatives.

The count trend supplies a meaningful problem rather than merely 'falling white cells'. No exact universal hold threshold is inferred from these constructed values. The explanation appropriately avoids asserting that mycophenolate is the proven sole cause.

The specific medication plans are comparably framed. 'Low' immunologic risk and 'appropriate' renal dosing are supplied judgments that narrow the choice but are necessary fairness boundaries here, not a nonmedical key match.

The standalone node includes current infection status, regimen, renal function and graft-risk context; it does not rely on the preceding CMV route question. This is high-yield competing drug-toxicity and treatment-efficacy reasoning.
suggestions: Keep the temporary/interim wording and explicit reassessment; do not turn this option into an automatic mycophenolate-stop rule for every declining count.

title: Crossmatch specimen and target after transfusion

cues.why: The update explicitly names the cell target that the resident is then asked to select. The options containing 'recipient lymphocyte controls' label themselves as controls rather than the requested donor crossmatch.

Combined with the explicit new post-transfusion antibody result, 'current' picks the newer serum and 'donor-directed' picks intended-donor lymphocytes. A reader can assemble the key by ordinary word/time matching without knowing the sensitization or crossmatch principles.

fairness: Post-transfusion recipient serum with intended-donor lymphocytes is the single defensible listed pairing for the requested current physical crossmatch. No confident clinical inaccuracy is identified.

The four-cell matrix is balanced, so component frequency does not create convergence. Its problem is that both dimensions are effectively specified in the wording; two components do not establish two consequential clinical inferences.
Transfusion sensitization and physical crossmatch orientation are high-yield foundations, but this exact item is easy matching rather than the requested resident application challenge.
The standalone record is coherent and includes both specimens and cell sources. The fixed six-week chronology is a constructed event, not an explicit universal sampling recommendation.
suggestions: Remove the instruction that a donor-cell crossmatch has already been requested and the contrastive 'controls' labeling from competing pairings; retain the actual specimens, cell identities and intervening sensitizing event.

Rebuild the task around a consequential interpretation or next compatibility action from actual pre/post-event results, with credible alternatives that require understanding sensitization and what the assay establishes. Do not simply obscure the words 'donor' and 'current'.
If only serum/cell identification is intended, seek explicit acceptance as a foundational item rather than label it a difficult two-step resident question.

title: Preconception regimen and readiness with changing graft function
clarityIssues: 'Begin conception attempts after that change' does not specify whether it means immediately after substitution or after an adequately completed preconception medication transition. That ambiguity adds a separate reason to reject the same options.

cues.phrase: begin conception attempts after that change
cues.why: If read as immediate attempts after replacing mycophenolate, these options can be rejected on medication-transition timing even after deleting the entire graft-instability record. That weakens the intended independent readiness inference; this is a clinical shortcut, not a purely lexical giveaway.

fairness: Azathioprine planning plus reassessment of graft stability is the best listed answer. The renal/protein trajectory and pregnancy-compatible regimen are both high-yield considerations, and the balanced matrix has no majority-component convergence.

The key is clinically reasonable; the concern is the temporal ambiguity of the distractors and incomplete teaching about readiness after mycophenolate withdrawal, not an asserted error in choosing azathioprine.

The explanation says it does not invent a washout interval, but that does not resolve what 'after that change' means. Do not manufacture an exact interval in this offline review; the required transition criteria need a supported clinician-reviewed formulation.

The standalone node supplies contraception, the regimen, time since transplant and changing graft function. It coherently asks about future planning rather than mandating an immediate switch during unexplained dysfunction.
Two consequential clinical dimensions are present, but the medication-timing alternative explanation should be removed before using this as a clean test of graft readiness.
suggestions: Make the same supported, adequately completed medication-transition condition explicit across all options, then distinguish proceeding despite the unresolved graft trajectory from waiting for reassessment.
Clarify that replacing mycophenolate alone does not establish immediate conception readiness; include a source-supported transition requirement without inventing a number.
Reapply the deletion test: the graft course must change the readiness answer after medication-transition timing is held constant.

title: Archived antibody investigation after an immediate graft event

cues.phrase: reconstructing the recipient's antibody state at implantation
cues.why: This explicitly states the specimen time to select, making 'preimplantation recipient serum' an ordinary time-word match. The plasma-exchange timing need not be interpreted to choose it.

Together with 'despite the negative HLA assessment' and options that simply repeat donor-specific HLA testing, 'additional' favors the only new antibody target. This is a completed-test versus new-test shortcut, even before interpreting the vascular injury.

fairness: Anti-A measurement in preimplantation/pre-exchange recipient serum is the best listed investigation for the separate ABO pathway raised by an A donor and O recipient. The explanation appropriately stops short of proving causation or inventing a diagnostic titer threshold.

The balanced matrix avoids frequency convergence, but most of the pathology can be deleted while preserving the key through the stated archival goal and already completed HLA assessment. The remaining ABO association is foundational recognition rather than two consequential steps.

ABO incompatibility and immediate antibody-mediated graft injury are high-yield concepts. The highly directed archival task makes this particular version easy; difficulty should not be manufactured by withholding a needed chronology.

The standalone retrospective record is coherent. Nothing here warrants a confident accusation that ABO-incompatible transplantation itself was improper; protocols, subgroups and acceptance thresholds are deliberately outside the task.
suggestions: Give the archive selection a real treatment-confounding inference instead of explicitly naming the desired preimplantation state in the update. Preserve the actual collection and exchange chronology.
Replace the already-completed HLA assessment as a disposable foil with comparably plausible unresolved investigations or interpretations, using supported clinical distinctions.
Ensure the observed graft event changes the requested decision; if the intended objective remains simple ABO target/specimen recognition, request an explicit foundational-purpose exception.

title: Treatment of active humoral injury after steroid nonresponse
fairness: Plasma exchange with IVIG is the best listed additional treatment backbone for the represented microvascular inflammation, C4d and donor-specific antibodies, without the described cellular or chronic glomerular component. The explanation appropriately labels the comparative evidence as weak.

The resident must reinterpret the repeat tissue rather than infer refractory cellular rejection from steroid failure, then choose mechanism-directed treatment. ATG is a credible anchoring error; maintenance reduction is an infection-pathway error.

The capillary findings and antibodies are necessary clinical observations, not a diagnosis label or direct phrase match to plasma exchange. Multiple negatives make the item moderate rather than hard but keep the competing treatment boundaries fair.
The standalone update supplies the prior course, current biopsy and background maintenance optimization. It does not depend on the earlier cellular rescue case.

Absence of glomerular double contours alone should not be taught as excluding every possible chronic AMR lesion. The text is limited to the represented tissue rather than a complete Banff classification; no confident key-changing inaccuracy is identified within this option set.
suggestions: Preserve the weak-evidence and acute-active scope qualifications; do not extend this backbone claim to all chronic active AMR.

title: Persistent delayed graft function after an earlier tubular-injury biopsy
fairness: Repeat allograft sampling is the best listed next assessment for persistent dialysis dependence/nonrecovery after an earlier tubular-injury specimen and the represented reassessment of reversible contributors. The earlier biopsy does not establish the current cause.

The resident interprets the age and limited temporal scope of tissue evidence, then decides to reassess rather than anchor on tubular injury or treat presumed rejection empirically. This is a high-yield delayed-function decision.

The supportive-care sentence applies to all options, preventing the biopsy answer from being the only comprehensive plan. 'Graft-assessment plan' mildly favors investigation, but monitoring is also an assessment strategy and the unresolved course justifies comparing assessment with empiric therapy.

The day-3/day-11 sequence is explicit and standalone. The explanation treats the dates as a constructed example and acknowledges low-quality interval-biopsy evidence rather than declaring a universal mandatory biopsy day.

Individual biopsy timing can vary with risk and prior findings; this offline review does not independently verify current interval guidance. Within the represented persistent nonrecovery and offered choices, no competing option is equally compelling.
suggestions: A neutral 'Which next plan best fits the postoperative course?' would remove the mild assessment-language bias without changing the clinical information.
